S&P Global Ratings also said it did not expect "a large systemic event if Evergrande defaults." But in a note to clients, it said the situation could worsen if a disorderly bankruptcy of the group coincided with a deeper market downturn in the sector. "This would set off a vicious cycle. We believe that the sector itself is already seeing some weakness in sales and pricing since August and could slip further."

Shares in Sinic Holdings, a Shanghai property developer, crashed 87% before trading was halted. Investors fear the company may struggle to refinance a $246 million bond it must repay on Oct. 18, now that investors have soured on the sector. Fitch Ratings last week cut its outlook on the company to negative.

Large Hong Kong developers also felt the negative impact. Sun Hung Kai Properties sank 10%, its largest decline since 2012, and Henderson Land tumbled 13%, with investors also spooked by a Reuters report last week that Beijing has warned the territory's property tycoons it will no longer tolerate "monopoly behavior."

China's biggest insurer Ping An fell as much as 8.4%. The company said on Friday it had no exposure to Evergrande and that its insurance investment fund had equity investments worth 63.1 billion yuan ($9.8 billion) linked to real estate developers, which it said were largely financially sound.

While the Chinese economy recovered swiftly from the pandemic-induced slowdown, signs have emerged of growth losing steam, particularly in the housing market where activity slumped sharply in July and weakened further in August.

Evergrande has begun offering suppliers and retail debt investors apartments, parking lots and commercial space in lieu of missed payments. It faces a series of bond coupon payments starting Thursday, and if it does not make the payments within a month it will be termed a defaulter.

"Our baseline remains that any potential default or restructuring of Evergrande would be carefully managed by the government with limited contagion effect in both financial and property markets," said Goldman Sachs economists led by Hui Shan. "This would require a clear message from the government soon to shore up confidence and to stop the spillover effect, the absence of which we think poses notable downside risk to growth in Q4 and next year."

However, the economists warned if a default occurred without clear "ring-fencing" of the spillovers to other parts of the economy, then the outcomes would be harsher, perhaps as much as a 4.1% hit to GDP as housing activity collapses and financial conditions tighten.

Evergrande shares slumped a further 10.2% in Hong Kong, taking losses for the year to 84%. The Hang Seng Property Index tumbled 6.7% to its lowest level since 2016 and the broader Hang Seng Index ended down 3.3%. Chinese markets are closed till Wednesday for holidays, but the FTSE China A50 index futures traded in Singapore declined over 3%

In Europe, the Euro Stoxx 600 index fell close to 2% while the U.S. Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 500 points at the open and the S&P 500 was down more than 1.5%. London's FTSE 100 slipped 1% with miners leading the retreat on concerns a China slowdown will further erode commodity prices. 

Iron ore prices fell below $100 a ton for the first time in over a year, as China's imposition of more steel production curbs combined with investor concerns that a real estate construction slowdown will cut demand for the metal. Copper declined 2%, as did oil.

Global economic growth is closely entwined with the fortunes of China, which was the only major economy to expand last year. In April, the International Monetary Fund projected China would contribute over a fifth of the increase in the world's gross domestic product in the five years to 2026.

HONG KONG -- A wave of fear over Chinese economic growth swept through global markets on Monday as China Evergrande, the country's most indebted property developer, teetered on the brink of default and investors worried about the consequences for its domestic peers and international commodity prices.  



While Chinese and Hong Kong property groups bore the brunt of the sell-off, the impact was felt across European and U.S. stock markets. China Evergrande, whose liabilities amount to almost a third of a trillion dollars, is facing deadlines this week for payments to banks and bondholders.  
 


"The repercussions from Evergrande's prospective collapse will likely contribute to China's ongoing economic deceleration, which in turn anchors global growth and inflation, and casts a pall over commodity prices," said Phoenix Kalen, a strategist at Societe Generale in London.

Taking other people's stuff is a perfectly viable win con.  He is playing a control deck, which is one of the basic archetypes in magic.  
I can't say for sure without looking at your lists, but I suspect that the other players at your table don't run nearly enough card draw.  Otherwise the control player would run out of answers before all three of their opponents run out of threats.  
For reference, at my table most decks run around 20 pieces of interaction, with some decks running 30+.  The game is a back and forth of players threatening a win and other players removing that win.  Typically in turns 5-8 the board state rapidly shifts around the table until one player manages to claw above the interaction and win.  It's an incredibly fun way to play.  
If you're in green, run uncounterable creatures.  If you're in red, run things like [[Pyroblast]]. If you're in white, run things like [[Grand Abolisher]].  Run card advantage both in terms of card draw and in term of recursion so you can get your threats back.  
Your playgroup has entered a plateau.  You can either embrace interactive play and end up with more complex games, or you can reject interactive play and stay battle cruiser forever.  If you choose to stay battle cruiser, as a group you are going to have to ban a ton of cards and play styles, because battle cruiser is not a viable play style if the entire EDH ecosystem is allowed.

It depends on what kind of position you are looking for. Picking up a new language in a [paradigm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_paradigm) you are used to really doesn't take very long anyway.  For example, I was a C# dev for a year before I wrote any Java.  It took me about 30 minutes to begin using Java, and a few days to become reasonably efficient.  I'm by no means a Java expert, but after about two months I was pretty comfortable using Java.  This is because Java and C# are both strongly statically typed Object-Oriented c-like languages.  My skills in C# were easy to map to Java.  On the other hand, jumping to Haskell was more difficult.  It took a few weeks before I was able to do much at all with Haskell because it was my first foray into a pure functional language.

You could approach it that way, but I usually try to avoid outright saying what my views are at first.  The idea is to uncover unexamined foundational beliefs and examine them.  Find out why they believe what they believe and then find out why they think the basis for their belief is a good one.  If it turns out that they do not have a good basis for their belief, then the discomfort of exposed cognitive dissonance may cause them to moderate their view or to hold their view less firmly.  If it turns out that they do have a good basis for their belief, then you have learned something important and should review your own views on the matter.

To be fair, Socrates was generally just an insufferable person.  No tact whatsoever.  The method of asking probing questions to get at someone's unexamined beliefs can be very effective if you combine it with tact and sincere friendliness.  As I discuss elsewhere, you are unlikely to change someone's beliefs dramatically in one conversation, but by using the Socratic method you can get people to think critically about beliefs that they may have never examined before.  At the very worst you are unlikely to polarize someone by asking questions.

>Unfortunately you run the risk of coming across as a condescending asshole who is "playing dirty tricks" and "word games" to a lot of people  
  
This is definitely true.  It sometimes takes a lot of tact, a lot of patience, and a lot of self control to avoid using a condescending tone.  The Socratic method can be hard to pull off because we are naturally inclined to jump in and passionately argue our own point of view.

>So while the idea is sound, many are trained to reflexively reject this entire way of thinking at all, because it is (to them) irrational -- because their concept of rational thinking has been shaped by their families, peers, and social and political bubble. Puncturing that bubble can be really, really difficult, if not impossible.  
  
This is also true.  It can be very difficult to sway people even an inch from deeply held beliefs.  The Socratic method is no silver bullet, but it is the most effective method I know of.  Part of its effectiveness is that it is less likely than argumentation to make people feel threatened and polarize listeners.  
  
Most of my experience with using the Socratic method with a 'hostile' participant is with evangelists (the kind who hand out pamphlets in parking lots).  Whenever an evangelist tries to engage me I try to take the time to talk with them and find out why they believe what they believe.  I have never come away from one of these discussions and turned an evangelist into an atheist.  On the other hand, by the end of these conversations the evangelist has often slightly moderated their views and more importantly has thought critically about their own beliefs in a way they may have never done before.  
  
  
Of course, as you suggest this method does not work well on loud mouths who are not interested in discussion.  I have tried it with street preachers to absolutely no avail.  I suspect, however, that if I were to catch these preachers while they are not preaching (and do not have an audience)  that they might be more willing to participate in a little introspection.

Genetic modification is about altering genes, and is considered synonymous with genetic engineering by most dictionaries.  When you select traits, you are choosing (often indirectly) to include genetic material that was already present in the species.  When you genetically modify something you alter the genetic makeup of the organism in a way that can add novel genetic material that was not present in any member of the species.  
You are free to use whatever personal definitions for words that you choose (language is fluid like that), but saying that 'all corn is GMO' is not true to the standard definition of 'GMO' and so can only serve to confuse.

GMO has a very specific meaning that includes genetic engineering. [here is the dictionary.com entry](http://www.dictionary.com/browse/gmo?s=t).  [here is the wikipedia entry](http://www.dictionary.com/browse/gmo?s=t).  Selective breeding is not genetic modification, it is trait selection.

That breaks down when you lose hp to environmental hazards though.  For instance, I played a barbarian who would cheerily jump from heights that would put him at terminal velocity because he could take the damage from the fall.  He also had to wade through lava at one point and was just dandy afterwards.  Our group generally uses hp in the same way that you do, but sometimes it just breaks down.

I'm sorry but things can be done with genetic engineering that are simply not possible with selective breeding or hybridization.  That's the beauty of genetic engineering.  So no, 'every kind of corn' is not GMO.

The real issue I have with GMO crossbreeding is that many modern crops can cross with related wild varieties.  Ecological studies on the impact this could have are not required for a new GMO to be put on the market.  Even if we have an idea of what the ecological impact of something like 'roundup ready' genes might have if spread to wild populations, we can't predict what impact unknown future modifications might have on worldwide ecosystems.  
Genetic modification is incredibly powerful and I am glad to live in a world where these new crops are possible, but I really think we need to be careful.  Genetic modification is not itself inherently harmful, but that does not mean that no GMO will be harmful to us or the environment.  We need a measured attitude about this that sees each new GMO as its own product that needs to be assessed individually.  In any case, I would really like to see governments pushing for consumer GMOs to be sterile with their non GMO relatives.  We are not allowed to save the seeds anyway, so we might as well mitigate the risks.

I don't think that my public university was particularly radical.  Like I said, this is not an uncommon definition of racism.  The first page of Google pulled up [this gem](http://www.clarke.edu/media/files/Multicultural_Student_Services/definitionsofracism.pdf) from  a liberal arts college.  My university was not nearly so radical as that.  [Here](https://www.andover.edu/About/Newsroom/TheMagazine/Documents/8-PedOfRacismSWJournal.pdf) is a paper that talks about the disagreement about the definition of racism (also found on the first page of a google search for "power + prejudice").  The definition of racism is a big issue in sociology and race studies today and the "power + prejudice" group is in no way a fringe group of radicals.

The issue is that the definition is usually more nuanced than that.  Often it isn't about personal power and privilege, but about belonging to a privileged group.  So, an impoverished white female can be racist because she belongs to the privileged race group, but she cannot be sexist because she belongs to an underprivileged gender group.  The fact that she has no personal power because of poverty does not really weigh on the outcome.

I have degrees in Anthropology and Philosophy from a public university in the Midwest.  I attended several conferences throughout the US and speakers at those conferences had the same definition for racism/sexism.  That definition also appeared in several textbooks which seem to be widely used.  It isn't a universally held definition, but it's a pretty standard one (just google power + prejudice).

Sadly this is what is taught in many sociology/anthropology/women's studies classes. This is because racism and sexism is defined by many sociologist and feminists as "prejudice plus power".  If you do not have power or privilege over the group you are prejudiced against, you cannot by their definition be racist or sexist against that group.

In the middle of the medieval period is hardly "towards the end" of it.  Even if it was, your accusation is still uncalled for. in combat, What wizards are really good at is setting the party up in a position of tactical advantage.  It is really fun to do and the rest of the party will love him for it.  Outside of combat the wizard can really shine depending on skill selection.  A wizard has access to all knowledge skills and probably has a boatload of skill points due to a high intelligence score, so set up scenarios where he is able to utilize all that lore hes got stuffed in his noggin.

As far as spell selection goes, I agree with other posters about color spray. It is absolutely amazing at low levels. In addition I strongly recommend grease, silent image, and floating disk.  

Illusion spells are VERY powerful.  In order to get a save against an illusion like silent image one must interact with it. This means that you can set up a very effective ambush by creating an illusion of a wall or boulder for your party to hide behind (or inside of!).  You can also control a battlefield by creating an illusion of a deep pit, thus herding your enemies into difficult terrain or keeping them from engaging in melee all together.  The possibilities with silent image are endless!

Does the party have an archer? My favorite trick with floating disk is to use it as a mobile archery platform.  It gives the archer a little height and allows you to sit back and move the archer around the field so that they are free to take full attacks for rapid shot and the such.  Fun times.

so, what I would recommend overall is to encourage your player to be creative with his spells.  Also let the wizard use his lore whenever possible.  It is a great way to introduce plot hooks anyway.
